title: Five facts about extreme poverty in the world in long time horizon: 1950-2050
gist: World Bank data show global extreme poverty fell from about 60% in 1950 to 10% in 2025, driven largely by China and India, but progress has stalled for a decade amid a polycrisis, with Sub-Saharan Africa stagnating and MENA worsening. Projections to 2050 range from 1.2% (Korea-pace) to around 8.5% on typical paths, with a risk that poverty rises again.

insights.claim: The share of the world population living in extreme poverty fell from about 60 percent in 1950 to 10 percent in 2025, even as global population more than tripled from 2.5 billion to 8.3 billion.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Long-run growth has dramatically expanded the global consumer base.

insights.claim: More than 800 million people still live in extreme poverty, defined as less than $3.00 a day in 2021 PPP terms.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Sizes the remaining extreme-poor population under the new poverty line.

insights.claim: Extreme poverty has been consistently low in Europe, North America and Latin America since 1990; rapid reduction came from East Asia and the Pacific and South Asia, while recent stagnation is driven by Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East and North Africa.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Poverty dynamics now hinge on Africa and MENA.
insights.locator: Extreme poverty has been consistently low

insights.claim: China went from about a billion people in extreme poverty in 1990 to almost none by 2015, and India's progress began about a decade later.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: China and India account for most of the historic gain in global purchasing power at the bottom.
insights.locator: The chart below shows the changes

insights.claim: Excluding China and India, global progress in reducing extreme poverty becomes much more modest.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Global poverty success is concentrated, implying limited spillover elsewhere.

insights.claim: Progress in reducing extreme poverty stalled in the past decade amid a polycrisis of COVID-19, more frequent and severe climate shocks, and geopolitical tensions such as Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Overlapping shocks have stalled development gains, weighing on frontier-market demand.

insights.claim: Once China had eradicated extreme poverty, the main engine of global reduction was exhausted, contributing to the slowdown.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Global poverty metrics now depend on harder-to-move regions.

insights.claim: Economic growth in Sub-Saharan Africa has been too low to compensate for high population growth, and conflicts in the Middle East worsened poverty in affected countries.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Per-capita growth is the key metric for African consumption stories.

insights.claim: The optimism behind the SDG goal of ending extreme poverty by 2030 has given way to stalled progress since the goals were adopted in 2015.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: The 2030 poverty target is effectively out of reach.

insights.claim: If current trajectories persist, little progress in extreme poverty will be seen until 2030 and extreme poverty is likely to increase by 2050.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: A rising poverty trend would signal structural weakness in the poorest economies.

insights.claim: If all countries replicated Korea's historical pace of poverty reduction, global extreme poverty would fall to 1.2 percent by 2050, though Korea's experience is exceptional.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: The optimistic scenario is unlikely to materialize.

insights.claim: Using the typical path observed since 1950, global extreme poverty would remain around 9.9 percent in 2030 and 8.5 percent in 2050; progress at Brazil's or Türkiye's pace would bring only gradual decline.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Base case implies slow change in global extreme poverty for decades.

insights.claim: Because poverty reduction has slowed sharply, the World Bank warns that if current trends continue the world could see extreme poverty start to rise again.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Reversal risk is a negative for development finance and frontier growth narratives.
insights.quote: if current trends continue, the world could see extreme poverty start to rise again.
